newsitem.title: USA: U.S. women voters swell gender gap for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: U.S. women voters swell gender gap for Clinton.

text.p: What do women want? A stable economy and a more caring government but not necessarily a tax cut, according to the results of the 1996 U.S. election, which showed the gender gap as a formidable political force.

The numbers tell the story: male voters were equally divided between President Bill Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole, giving 44 percent of their votes to each candidate. But among women, Clinton was the clear victor with 54 percent of the female vote; Dole got 37 percent.

Both Clinton's Democrats and Dole's Republicans courted women this year, but their varying interpretation of what constituted a "women's issue" made the difference, said Irene Natividad, head of Women's Vote Project '96 which worked to get more women to the polls.

Attempts to make the amorphous "family values" resonate with women failed, Natividad said, and the centrepiece of the Dole campaign -- a promised 15 percent tax cut aimed at helping American families to make ends meet -- was also ineffective.
"The women were the most dubious about the tax cuts," Natividad said. "Clearly that message didn't wash.
The Clinton team's 1992 campaign message -- "It's the economy, stupid" -- played well with women then and now, but the economy itself had shifted to benefit the sitting president.

During Clinton's first run for the White House, he pointed to a sluggish economy and vowed to re-invigorate it. This year, with most economic indicators bullish and most of the electorate content, the economy redounded to his credit; Dole's bid to ripple the economic waters was swamped by a flood of relatively fiscal good news.

Abortion rights groups, including the National Abortion and Reproductive Rights Action League and Planned Parenthood, hailed the re-election of Clinton and the election of abortion rights proponents in Congress, but abortion was not one of the key issues this year, Natividad said.
"The abortion issue played a role but not necessarily a major role," she said, noting that few women listed this as their first concern, though it might be a deciding factor in some contests.

Instead, women chose education and crime as key issues, and Clinton exploited this by raising fears that Republican candidates would cut education programmes and stressed his own support for 100,000 new police on U.S. streets.

There was another factor helping Clinton and Democrats running for Congress, and this was the perception of mean-spiritedness among the 1994 class of so-called Republican revolutionaries headed by House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia. More women than men were repelled by this feeling, Natividad said.

In terms of gains for female candidates, this year's elections were mixed. New Hampshire got its first-ever female governor and two new women joined the Senate. But since the Senate lost two women, one by retirement and one by a loss in a primary election, the number of women in the Senate will stay stable at nine.
Many races in the House (of Representatives) were too close to call on Wednesday.
But even though the number of women in office may not change much, Natividad said women's influence changed the face of American politics in 1996.
"This was a kinder, gentler election because of the fear of the reactions of women voters," she said. "The dialogue used by the candidates was intended to appeal to women."
